output.headline: Women's testimony leads jury to convict Russell Brand of rape and assault
output.bodyHtml:
Russell Brand has been found guilty of raping a fan and sexually assaulting three other women, after a trial that heard how the women had been haunted by their encounters with the former presenter and had bravely come forward to tell the truth after realising they were not alone. The verdicts end a years-long legal saga that has raised questions about how Brand was able to commit his crimes at the height of his fame.

Brand, 51, was described during his trial as a ruthless, calculated and manipulative sexual predator. He was convicted of raping a woman at his luxury London townhouse and of sexually assaulting women in front of his entourage at their workplaces, at a radio station and TV studio.

After the trial, the victims' commissioner for England and Wales, Claire Waxman, warned against the perpetuation of rape myths in the legal system, noting that part of Brand's defence had rested on the claim that "not one of [the victims] resisted or screamed or even tried to leave". “The idea that rape victims must scream, physically resist or immediately report an offence is a well-established rape myth, rooted in outdated and harmful assumptions about how victims are expected to behave,” she said. “Justice must be grounded in evidence, not misconceptions.”

The Hollywood actor turned online influencer was accused of gaslighting his victims after the attacks, and treating women as a “disposable commodity” and a “means to an end” to satisfy his voracious sexual appetite.

The prosecutor, Riel Karmy-Jones KC, said the women described a similar pattern of behaviour from the comedian that started with compliments, flattery and flirting before a “personality change”. “His eyes changed, he snapped, from charming to frightening to nasty,” she said.

It can now be revealed that Brand is under investigation for two further rape allegations and that the Metropolitan police have submitted files to the Crown Prosecution Service. On Thursday the Met said its investigation into Brand was continuing.

Brand – who will be sentenced on Monday – stood outside the door of the dock shortly before the jury delivered their verdicts and looked at his wife, Laura, saying: “Laura, I love you.”

Wearing a grey three-piece suit, he appeared to be praying in the dock before he was convicted of four offences on Thursday after a four-week trial at Southwark crown court.

He had pleaded not guilty to three charges of rape, three of sexual assault and one of attempted indecent assault against six women, in allegations spanning 10 years from 1999.

Brand had claimed he could not remember some of the incidents, and that others had been consensual sexual encounters that had been “reimagined” or “unfavourably reframed” after the publication of sexual misconduct allegations against him in a 2023 Channel 4 Dispatches documentary, and Times and Sunday Times reports.

Brand closed his eyes as a jury found him guilty of four offences against four women after eight hours and 30 minutes of deliberations. He was cleared of two counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault.

The judge, Mr Justice Bennathan, praised the panel of four women and eight men, and told Brand: “You've been convicted of a number of offences, including one of rape. The consequence of that is inevitably a significant custodial term. My current view is that I have to therefore remand you in custody.”

Brand appeared emotionless as he was led away by the dock officers down to the cells. His wife was visibly upset and left the court soon after.

His barrister, Ian Winter KC, made a plea for Brand to be given bail over the weekend as an “act of humanity” so that he could say goodbye to his children, but the judge refused.

Bennathan said he regretted the “hardship” caused to the children but said: “Whatever the good intentions of the family and the defendant today, I think there are substantial grounds to fear he might in the end not feel able to come along and face his sentence.”

As the judge remanded him into custody, Brand made “OK” gestures and said: “I'm good, I'm good, I'm good,” before being taken out of the dock.

Brand was found guilty of anally raping a young fan at his London townhouse after picking her out from a crowd after one of his gigs at the Hammersmith Apollo in early 2009.

She told the court she had begged him to stop but Brand had continued. “I felt like I couldn't speak or breathe, the amount of pain,” she said.

He was also found guilty of sexually assaulting a woman who worked for MTV by grabbing her breasts at a birthday party in Soho, London in 2004. But he was cleared of orally raping the woman in a toilet afterwards.

He was also convicted of sexually assaulting a woman who told the court that Brand had laughed after squeezing her breasts and kissing her sloppily while she was working at the radio station Choice FM in 2004 or 2005.

Brand was found guilty of sexually assaulting a Channel 4 worker, who said she had been “repulsed” when Brand placed his head in her lap so she could feel his breath on her “vagina” during a filming project in 2009.

He was cleared of raping a woman at the Labour party conference in Bournemouth in 1999, and also found not guilty of attempting to indecently assault an MTV worker by trying to drag her into a men's toilets in 2001.

Brand's barrister denied the TV personality was a “psychopath who rapes people and thinks it's normal”. The barrister also said that the 2023 media reports had “poisoned the well” of justice, and rendered it impossible for Brand to have a fair trial.

Outside the courtroom there was an extraordinary exchange between Winter and the Sunday Times journalist Rosamund Urwin, who was involved in the 2023 investigation.

He said to Urwin: “I hope you are pleased with yourself.” After she replied: “I'm pleased justice has been done,” Winter said: “Well, it wasn't. You fucked it.” He then added: “Congratulations.”

Brand's case has led to difficult questions for the BBC, Channel 4 and the production companies that worked with him. The TV world is again asking itself whether recent efforts to improve safeguarding will stop similar abuses.

In a statement on Thursday, Channel 4 said: “We recognise the profound impact of these crimes and commend the extraordinary courage of all those who gave evidence as prosecution witnesses at trial.”

A BBC spokesperson said that a 2025 report had examined how complaints about Brand's conduct were handled, looking at eight allegations from his time at the BBC, and added: “It was of great concern to us that some people felt unable to raise concerns about Brand's behaviour. We apologised to those impacted, for both the culture and failings at the time, and we reiterate that apology again today.”

• Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organisations. In the UK, Rape Crisis offers support on 0808 802 9999 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 in Scotland, or 0800 0246 991 in Northern Ireland. In the US, Rainn offers support on 800-656-4673. In Australia, support is available at 1800Respect (1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found at ibiblio.org/rcip/internl.html
output.standfirst:
Women's testimony persuaded a jury that Russell Brand, 51, raped one woman and sexually assaulted three others between 2004 and 2009; he was remanded ahead of a 'significant' prison term.

  • Flashbulbs, lies and victim blaming: how Russell Brand's trial unfolded

  • The downfall of Russell Brand: from Big Brother and Hollywood to convicted rapist
output.progress: The Metropolitan Police are investigating two further rape allegations against Brand, with case files submitted to prosecutors.

output.headline: Attorney general's challenge secures longer sentence for Henry Nowak's killer
output.bodyHtml:
Henry Nowak's killer has seen his sentence extended by the court of appeal after it ruled that his original sentence was “unduly lenient”.

Vickrum Digwa's original sentence of life with a minimum term of 21 years was lengthened to a minimum of 24 years and 190 days after a successful appeal by the attorney general, Ellie Reeves.

Reeves said: “The brutality and cruelty of this case horrified me, and I know that feeling is shared by the British public. I welcome the court of appeal's decision to increase the minimum term of Digwa's life sentence.”

Digwa, 23, stabbed Nowak several times in an attack in Southampton in December last year.

When police arrived at the murder scene, Digwa falsely claimed Nowak had racially abused him and knocked his turban off, causing officers to arrest and handcuff Nowak before they saw his fatal injuries.

Digwa filmed his victim as he lay dying and lied to emergency services that Nowak, 18, had racially abused him.

The incident led to riots in Southampton.

Lady Chief Justice Carr said the original sentencing judge, William Mousley KC, had materially understated two distinct dimensions of Digwa's offending.

She said: “First, the circumstances in which a large and immediately available dagger was used repeatedly with an intention to kill an unarmed man, and secondly, the deliberate cruelty, additional suffering, and obstruction [of justice] which followed the stabbing.”

She added: “A minimum term of 21 years did not adequately reflect the overall seriousness of the murder. It was not only lenient, but unduly so.

“Therefore, we quash the minimum term of 21 years. We replace it with a minimum term of 25 years. From that term must be deducted the 175 days spent in custody on remand, producing an operative minimum term of 24 years and 190 days.”

In written submissions on behalf of Reeves, Jonathan Polnay KC said the sentence failed to take into account a series of “significant aggravating factors”, including Digwa's “false allegation of racism against the deceased” and his “abuse” of the privilege afforded to Sikhs to carry a knife in a public place for religious reasons.

At Digwa's sentencing hearing, Mousley said that on the night of the murder, Digwa had a small knife hidden from view called a kirpan, which is a strict requirement for Sikhs to carry at all times.

Digwa also had a “large dagger in a sheath” due to his membership of the Nihang, an order of Sikhs which has a tradition of holding a second knife.

Polnay told the court that the attempt to increase the sentence was “not about the lawful possession of a kirpan” and the laws allowing Sikhs to carry blades. “It is about what followed.” He said Digwa's use of the dagger was “on at least one level, analogous to an abuse of trust”.

He continued: “When a person who has the benefit of that accommodation uses the article protected by law for repeated lethal violence, that is an aggravating factor of particular weight.”

Polnay also cited “the offender's sustained attempts to pervert the course of justice” and “his procurement of his mother's assistance in concealing evidence”.

Digwa's mother, Kiran Kaur, 53, was jailed for three years for assisting an offender by taking the knife from where her son murdered Novak back to the family home.

Polnay said other aggravating factors included Digwa's “degradation of the dying victim by filming him, and his conduct in misleading responders”.

His submission said: “The minimum term imposed failed adequately to reflect the combined weight of those features.”

In her ruling made alongside Mr Justice Nicklin and Mr Justice Wall, Carr said: “A person who knowingly carries a large knife or other bladed article in public, even if lawfully, and then uses it to kill an unarmed man after only a brief altercation, is highly culpable. His culpability is much closer to that of a person who takes a weapon into the street for offensive use than to that of someone who kills without a weapon, or someone who picks up a weapon of opportunity.”

On the false allegations of racism, Carr said: “It is unnecessary for us to determine whether the allegation of racial abuse was false, for even if that finding is left out of account, it does not affect our assessment of the appropriate minimum term.”

Digwa watched proceedings from HMP Frankland in County Durham, wearing a dark suit, shirt and tie.

Members of Nowak's family attended the hearing at the Royal Courts of Justice, with one relative wiping their eyes as the ruling was handed down.

Imran Khan KC, for Digwa, said the sentence could be increased only in “exceptional, rather than borderline cases, and directed to gross error by the sentencing judge”. He asked: “Where is the gross error?”

Challenging the length of the sentence, Khan said that while Digwa's lies to first responders “unquestionably affected the dignity with which Mr Nowak was treated”, his wounds were unsurvivable. “The false account therefore did not worsen the fatal injury or deprive Mr Nowak of the prospect of survival,” he said.

In response to Digwa's appeal, Carr said: “Having reached the conclusion that the proper minimum term would be at least 25 years, we refuse Digwa leave to appeal against his sentence. It is unarguable that it is manifestly excessive.”
output.standfirst: The court of appeal ruled Vickrum Digwa's original 21-year minimum term for murdering Southampton teenager Henry Nowak was 'unduly lenient' and raised it after an appeal by the attorney general, Ellie Reeves.

output.headline: Philippine investigators expect answer within days on Markle Jr’s alleged role in abuse case
output.bodyHtml:
Thomas Markle Jr, the Duchess of Sussex’s estranged half-brother, has been named a “person of interest” in the Philippine authorities’ inquiry into child sexual abuse image allegations made against her father, Thomas Markle Sr.

The country’s interior and local government secretary, Jonvic Remulla, said investigators expect to resolve the question soon, telling a press conference in Manila: “We’re determining if [the] son is involved … There are signs that point that the son is involved in the crime as well but only as a person of interest so far.” He added: “We will know in the next few days.”

It was Markle Jr himself who first alerted the authorities: he reported his father after claiming to have found four storage boxes at his father’s home in the Philippines containing “hundreds, if not thousands” of child sex abuse images.

Remulla had earlier told the same news conference there were “signs that point that the son is involved in the crime as well”.

Markle Jr, 60, who alerted local police and the FBI to images he found in his father’s belongings, was not yet being treated as a suspect. His alleged involvement is not thought to be directly linked to the material he handed to the police.

Markle Jr was recently interviewed at his home in Cordova, Cebu, as part of an international, multi-agency meeting via Microsoft Teams, according to the Sun, which first published the claims. He gave his statement to an FBI agent based in Florida, who specialises in child sex abuse cases.

Police and FBI agents have since been investigating whether Markle Sr was in possession of any illegal images while living in the Philippines and in Mexico, where he previously lived, and where other illegal images were reportedly found in one of his storage units.

More than 7,000 photos and one video – all of under-age males and females of Asian, Latin and European descent, with some as young as 10 and 11 – were uncovered, Remulla said.

He described the images as “the most deplorable displays of impunity towards sexual activity that I have ever seen”.

Remulla has previously described Markle Sr as “a possible sex offender of the grossest kind”.

Markle Sr, 82, who is estranged from Meghan, has reportedly been moved into a care home for dementia patients in the US, where he is now living.

Markle Sr, who returned to the US from the Philippines in May, has admitted paying for sex in the Philippines but he has strongly denied possessing child abuse imagery, and suggested he had been “set up”. His son remains in Cebu City in the Philippines.

In a statement issued when the allegations against her father were first published, Meghan said she was “deeply distressed” by the claims. She said she had been informed of disturbing allegations against her father in 2018 and had kept him from having contact with her children, Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five, to protect them.
output.standfirst: Philippine investigators say they expect an answer within days on whether Thomas Markle Jr — a person of interest, not a suspect — was involved in the child sexual abuse imagery case against his father, Thomas Markle Sr.

output.headline: Multi-agency search finds nothing suspicious after wave of hoax calls
output.bodyHtml:
Flights across Europe by Ryanair, Aer Lingus, Wizz Air, Finnair, easyJet, Aegean Airlines, Iberia, Sky Express, Air Serbia and LOT Polish Airlines all landed safely this week after a wave of hoax bomb threats, with searches of the planes finding nothing suspicious.

Hoax bomb threats disrupted at least 34 flights across Europe this week, with some forced to make emergency landings, as questions mount over an apparently coordinated effort to cause chaos for travellers.

At least 25 bomb threats affected flights on Thursday between Italy, Ireland, the UK, Spain, Bulgaria, Romania, Poland, Finland, Austria, Denmark, Belgium, Portugal, France, Greece, Serbia and Czechia.

In the UK, Heathrow, London’s principal airport, and Birmingham airport received threats overnight, but it was determined that they were hoaxes with the help of specialist investigators from the Metropolitan police’s aviation police command.

The Met said threats had been made against four aircraft departing from or arriving at Heathrow. A police spokesperson added that, after an assessment, “no security issues [were] identified”.

Related: Why have more than 30 European flights been hit by bomb threats this week?

Investigators said on Thursday there remained no evidence that the hoaxes were being orchestrated by a hostile terror group or state actor, such as Russia or Iran, although inquiries across Europe into the incidents continue.

The day of hoaxes followed similar threats on Tuesday, when seven planes across Europe were searched or diverted after malicious alerts. On Monday a flight from the UK to Bulgaria was diverted after a threat that was apparently without substance.

The global airlines body Iata condemned the disruption and urged authorities to identify the origin of the threats. “Safety is the number one priority for the industry and we take all threats seriously,” said Nick Careen, Iata’s senior vice-president for operations, safety and security, in a statement.

The EU transport commissioner, Apostolos Tzitzikostas, said it was too early to know if the incidents were linked but that any threats against civilians were unacceptable.

While getting a large explosive onboard should be ruled out by multiple layers of security and screening, the effects of any detonation would be multiplied for planes at typical cruising altitude of 35,000ft.

Aviation experts say fake threats occur daily but that such a number of credible threats, even if malicious hoaxes, appears to point to coordinated action.

Bomb threats emailed to airports in Rome and Sofia were signed “fighters of the Male State”, according to sources at Aeroporti di Roma, which manages the city’s two airports, and a text seen by Agence France-Presse.

Male State is a Russian far-right, ultranationalist and misogynistic movement founded in 2016 by Vladislav Pozdnyakov. On his Telegram channel Pozdnyakov, a prominent supporter of the war in Ukraine, did not comment on or claim responsibility for the bomb threats.

The emails reportedly read: “We, the fighters of the Male State, will make history with our actions today. Your feminist regime will remember this for ever. The explosion will occur in 60 minutes. Today, your skies will turn red.”

A Cork airport spokesperson confirmed to the Guardian that the airport had received an anonymous threat by phone on Thursday morning, causing a flight to be delayed. It was understood to be a Ryanair flight from London Stansted.

A separate Ryanair flight from Pescara in Italy to Brussels-Charleroi was inspected after the word “bomb” was discovered scrawled on the walls of its onboard toilet.

The affected flights had knock-on effects but were a tiny fraction of the 27,400 flights scheduled in Europe on Thursday, according to the European air traffic control agency, Eurocontrol.

The pilot of an Aer Lingus flight from Dublin to Rome that diverted to Évreux was being questioned by French authorities for initially refusing to land at a military base, according to French media reports.

The disruption followed cyber-attacks this week against supermarket refrigeration systems.

Related: Tell us: have you been affected by the bomb threats to flights in Europe?

A Kremlin spokesperson said on Thursday it was “absurd” to blame Vladimir Putin’s administration for the fridge hacks. “We have ​​such baseless accusations against our country, implicating it in everything,” Dmitry Peskov told reporters.

In Rome, Guido Crosetto, the Italian defence minister, said: “It seems to me that every day now, from refrigerators to blood supplies in France, to these fake alarms, there’s someone who has an interest in stoking tensions.”

Asked if he knew who was behind the hoaxes, he said: “It’s called ‘under-threshold warfare’ because it’s below the attribution threshold. It’s done that way on purpose, so no one can pin the blame.”

Many of the affected flights were operated by low-cost carriers but there was little discernible pattern surrounding the incidents.

Diversions are expensive as well as highly disruptive, but airlines have little choice in the face of any remotely credible threat.

The ready availability of airline operations information on the internet means that any hoaxer now has a level of detail about the schedules, the type of plane and its technical specifications that would have eluded all but insiders decades ago.

Rhys Jones, an analyst at Osprey Flight Solutions, an aviation intelligence firm, said the confidence of airlines in European airport security should not mean any change to normal protocols after the hoaxes, but “one of the natural responses will be to see double-downed security, media coverage and public concern about travelling”.

He said the threats seemed linked but “a reasonably chaotic campaign with no particular region targeted”, and while they could weaken future security responses through the normalisation of threats, simply creating disruption could be regarded as a success by those carrying out the hoaxes.

Additional reporting by Pjotr Sauer in Amsterdam and Angela Giuffrida in Rome
output.standfirst: Dozens of flights across Europe were diverted or searched this week after an apparently coordinated wave of hoax bomb threats; Thursday's batch of affected flights all landed safely, with searches finding nothing suspicious.
output.progress: Police, aviation security teams and European agencies are investigating the hoaxes, with the airline body Iata and the EU both condemning the disruption and demanding answers.

output.headline: Review recommends fewer, stronger police forces, sources say
output.bodyHtml:
Police are heading for failure unless England and Wales's 43 forces are reshaped into a smaller, stronger set, with the ability to catch criminals and rebuild public confidence at risk otherwise, Britain's most senior police officer will say on Friday.

Sir Mark Rowley, the Metropolitan police commissioner, is among the chiefs behind the stark comments, which come as some police leaders demand a radical package of reforms.

According to multiple sources, a government-ordered review has concluded that England's police forces should be consolidated from 39 to as few as nine "super forces".

The review was carried out by the former Met police commissioner Bernard Hogan-Howe and is yet to be published.

Sources say the plan under consideration would create nine regional forces, plus a single force for Wales, sitting above more than 150 local policing units that would carry out most neighbourhood crime-fighting.

Rowley and other chiefs who back the most radical change to policing in seven decades, and who regard axing most of the 43 forces in England and Wales as essential, are concerned that the government may delay it.

Hogan-Howe completed the review in September and sent it to the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood. Government sources say it will be published before Christmas, with a white paper to follow in the new year.

The delay is understood to reflect Andy Burnham's devolution agenda and his desire to "rewire" the British state and reform local government, including adding more mayors.

One police source said: "There are some concerns Andy Burnham may want to align the new police structures with mayors, which could mean 20 or more forces. That is not a radical enough change."

Rowley, Greater Manchester's chief constable Sir Stephen Watson and other chiefs will press for a reduction in the number of forces at an event in Manchester on Friday.

The event, titled "The cost of standing still is that criminals will win", has drawn criticism from other chief constables, who have told the Guardian they are annoyed by the Met-organised gathering and are sceptical of, or do not support, the reduction to as few as nine forces.

Reducing the number of forces in England and Wales is the centrepiece of Mahmood's radical changes to policing, and multiple sources say Hogan-Howe's report sets out a range for the new, larger forces, from nine to 18.

In his speech, Rowley will point to a fall in public confidence and say that positive outcomes – that is, crimes detected by officers that lead to a charge, caution, out of court settlement or no further action – "are now less than half what they were 12 years ago".

According to extracts released before the speech, Rowley will say: "I believe this is a choice between the third greatest revolution in British policing or the inevitable decline and fewer bobbies on the beat."

He will call for the 43 forces in England and Wales to be cut to eight or 10, adding: "Policing has tried to keep up, made do as best it can to patch over our broken model … But the model is creaking. We have 43 overstretched forces trying to do too much with too little."

Hogan-Howe believes the changes would free up policing to innovate rapidly as new crime types and threats emerge, after criticism that the current model of 43 forces, each overseen by its own police and crime commissioner, is too slow and delivers a postcode lottery of varying service for crime victims.

Hogan-Howe came out publicly in favour of a reduction to nine forces 12 years ago.

The bigger forces would handle major crimes – such as murders and serious sexual violence – and public order, as well as expensive but essential back-office functions such as human resources, currently done by each of the 43 forces individually.

Above the regional forces would sit a new nationwide force called the National Police Service, which the government wants to be the home of counter-terrorism policing and serious and organised crime. The advert for a commissioner for the national force is expected to be issued early in the new year.

Police leaders are divided on the scale of reduction: some favour voluntary mergers, while the new white paper would allow ministers to enforce the mass abolition of forces and creation of new ones.

Related: What is Shabana Mahmood proposing in 'biggest ever' policing reforms?

The changes could create a vast south-east England force stretching from the London borders to the southern coast of England, and a new north-west force extending from the Mersey to the Pennines, covering Greater Manchester, Merseyside and Lancashire, as well as smaller forces such as Cheshire and Cumbria.

One chief constable told the Guardian: "Everyone knows 43 forces have to go. But the return on investment could take five or six years."

Another chief constable said: "If I was the chief constable of the super force, it would be such a huge area, I wouldn't know anybody. I worry about it being too big."

Matthew Scott, the Conservative police and crime commissioner for Kent, said: "They will spend a great deal of time tearing up the fabric of policing for a suboptimal outcome." The government plans to abolish PCCs as part of its changes.

Another police leader asked: "Where is the evidence bigger forces are better?" They cited the fact that in recent years the largest – such as the Met, Greater Manchester and West Midlands – had failed so badly they had been put into special measures and their chief constables or commissioners had been ousted.

Scotland and Northern Ireland are each already covered by a single force.
output.standfirst: Mark Rowley wants England and Wales's 43 forces cut to as few as eight to 10, as a separate government review considers cutting England's 39 forces to as few as nine; Rowley will warn that public confidence is falling and crime detection rates have halved.
output.progress: The government says it will publish the Hogan-Howe review before Christmas, with a white paper to follow in the new year.

output.headline: Specialist isolation care limits risk after UK doctor's Ebola evacuation
output.bodyHtml:
A British doctor who contracted Ebola while helping the response to the outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has returned to the UK for specialist treatment.

The patient, whose identity is unknown, is now being cared for in a specialised high-level isolation unit at the Royal Free hospital in Hampstead, north London, after being transported home on a medical evacuation flight, the Department of Health and Social Care said on Thursday.

Dr Renu Bindra, the deputy director for all-hazards public health response at the UK Health Security Agency, said: "UKHSA and the NHS have well-established and robust infection prevention and control protocols to limit the risk of onward transmission, and the risk to the wider public remains low."

The doctor had been sent to DR Congo by a humanitarian organisation to help the response to the outbreak, which is the second largest on record, and is the first case of a British national contracting Ebola during it.

The Royal Free's isolation unit has strict protocols in place to prevent the patient coming into contact with any members of the public, and all staff treating the patient are equipped with the necessary personal protective equipment alongside other measures to prevent transmission.

Ebola is a highly contagious, severe and often fatal illness spread through direct contact with body fluids such as the blood or vomit of infected people, or dead bodies.

The current outbreak, declared in May by DR Congo's health ministry, has surpassed 10,000 cases and 5,000 deaths. It has spread to Kenya and Uganda in east Africa, and last month Nigeria confirmed a case in its capital, Abuja.

People with the disease tend to fall ill two to 21 days after contact with an orthoebolavirus. Initial symptoms include fever, aches, pains, and fatigue, but can then progress to diarrhoea, vomiting and unexplained bleeding.

There have only been four confirmed cases of the virus in the UK previously. A case in 1976 was from a laboratory needle incident, and the three others involved health workers who were responding to an outbreak in West Africa between 2014 and 2015.
output.standfirst: A doctor is being treated in a specialist isolation unit at London's Royal Free hospital, with officials saying the risk to the public remains low, after catching Ebola while helping fight the outbreak in DR Congo.
output.progress: UKHSA and the NHS say well-established infection control protocols are in place at the Royal Free to limit the risk of the virus spreading further.

output.headline: Early cancer diagnoses rise as NHS brings tests closer to patients
output.bodyHtml:
More cancers in England are now being caught at an early stage, even as a record 1,021 people a day were diagnosed with cancer in 2024: according to the latest NHS figures, 56.7% of new cancers were diagnosed at stage 1 or 2, up from 55.8% in 2023.

Prof Peter Johnson, the NHS national clinical director for cancer, said the figures showed the health service was “moving in the right direction” and were testimony to NHS staff’s hard work.

He said: “NHS teams across the country are taking tests and checks closer to the people who need them, and with new treatments being developed all the time, we will continue to do all we can to get people seen and treated for cancer as early as possible.”

Cancer diagnoses in England have also hit record highs, with more than 1,000 people a day diagnosed, the figures show.

But experts warned that although the health service was identifying more cases, it was still failing to meet timescale targets on diagnosis and treatment.

According to the latest cancer registration statistics, more than 373,000 people were diagnosed with cancer in England in 2024, the highest figure on record. On average, NHS England diagnosed 1,021 people a day with cancer in 2024, up from 972 a day in 2023.

Prostate, breast, lung and bowel cancers accounted for half of all new diagnoses.

Experts urged caution, however, given the NHS is failing to meet its timescale targets. The latest monthly NHS figures show that 78.6% of patients in England urgently referred for suspected cancer were diagnosed or had cancer ruled out within 28 days in August – below the target of 80%.

The health service is lagging even further behind on treatment. The proportion of patients who began treatment for cancer within 62 days of an urgent referral or consultant upgrade was 71.9%, well below the target of 85%.

Dr Ian Walker, the executive director of policy at Cancer Research UK, said: “While NHS staff are diagnosing more people with cancer every day, too many are still being caught at a late stage.”

The health service needed additional support to reduce the number of cancers diagnosed at a late stage and treat patients on time, he added.

Walker said: “The UK government pledged to improve early diagnosis, cancer waiting times and access to treatment in its national cancer plan for England. It now needs to keep its foot on the pedal to ensure cancer patients aren’t let down. The situation won’t change without focused effort from the government, clear accountability, and a guarantee that the NHS will get the specialist staff and equipment it needs.”

Dr Hilary Williams, the clinical vice-president at the Royal College of Physicians and a consultant in medical oncology, said: “More than 1,000 cancer diagnoses every day is a stark reminder of the growing demand on NHS cancer services.

“An ageing population is an important factor in the increase in diagnoses, but we must also recognise the role of obesity, which is a major and often overlooked risk factor for cancer.” She added that alongside preventing cancer, the NHS needed to continue improving early detection, including through the expansion of targeted lung cancer screening.

Related: Ethnic minorities in England less likely to get breast cancer diagnosis from routine screening

Williams said: “As more people are diagnosed and live longer with cancer, we must ensure they can access the specialist care and support they need.”

Steven McIntosh, the chief partnerships officer at Macmillan Cancer Support, said the figures also masked persistent health inequalities. “We know that who you are and where you live can still have a significant impact on how likely you are to get cancer, as well as how quickly you are diagnosed and your chances of survival,” he said.

Rachael Franklin, the deputy chief executive of Breast Cancer Now, said with diagnoses at an all-time high and overall incidence increasing, “breast cancer remains the biggest killer of working-age women in the UK, with one in seven women diagnosed in their lifetime”.

“That’s why it’s so important that people of all ages are breast aware and get anything new or unusual checked by a GP as soon as possible. We also urge all eligible women to attend their screening appointment when invited,” she said.
output.standfirst: The proportion of cancers diagnosed early edged up in 2024, as NHS England diagnosed a record 1,021 people a day — though the service is still missing its diagnosis and treatment speed targets, experts say.
output.progress: The Royal College of Physicians is calling for the expansion of targeted lung cancer screening to help catch cases earlier.

output.headline: Trump cites repairs as he locks in protection for his gold Oval Office
output.bodyHtml:
Donald Trump says he has paid for repairs and hired skilled workers to restore the White House’s exterior after years of deterioration, pointing to cracked windows, damaged stonework and broken decorative features that needed fixing.

“When you looked at that wall one year ago, it was badly damaged from years of service,” he said, adding that exterior columns had also been in “horrible shape”.

On Thursday, as part of the same renovation push, Trump signed a proclamation that he says will prevent future administrations from changing his design of the Oval Office and Cabinet Room, spaces which he declared as national monuments that should be preserved.

In the days since his party suffered historic defeats in the midterm elections, the president has seemingly turned his attention to the many renovation projects he has begun across the nation’s capital. Sitting behind the Resolute Desk on Thursday, Trump declared the Oval Office a “national monument”.

“I’m going to be signing a document which will make them into a landmark for the ages,” he told reporters in the gold-covered Oval Office.

According to the president, the proclamation would ensure the West Wing rooms would not be “touched by anybody, destroyed, ripped down by stupid people, in order to build something in a slightly different shape”.

“I just thought it was very important that nobody be allowed to come and take it down and try and do something with it,” he said.

“Every once in a while they’ll look and they’ll say, oh, maybe what we’ll do is we’ll put some glass up that’s a little bit better or something, and I say no, you’re not going to do anything. We’re going to leave this as it is,” he continued.

“If anyone ever decides to come and start knocking down walls, you’ll call me wherever I may be, and I will come back here and I will make sure it never happens.”

Since returning to office, Trump has embarked on a series of White House “beautification” projects, most notably the demolition of the East Wing to make way for a $600m ballroom, as well the building of a permanent granite helipad on the South Lawn.

On the desk next to where he signed the proclamation was a red baseball cap emblazoned with the word “Veto” – an explicit reminder of his threat to block the legislative priorities and bills passed by the new Democratic-controlled Congress next year.

Democrats made significant gains in several traditionally Republican states where Trump had previously won, including Texas, Kansas, South Carolina and Iowa, by campaigning on issues including affordability and tackling corruption, while also securing control of Congress.

Trump’s opulent redesign of the Oval Office has drawn criticism, including from former president Barack Obama, who recently joked that “he’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory. Just gold everywhere.”

Obama’s remark prompted a coordinated response from the White House, with treasury secretary Scott Bessent appearing to hit back by dining at a Cheesecake Factory.

In a final appeal ahead of the midterm elections, Trump held a press conference highlighting the delayed results of his $14m renovation of the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool, while blaming Joe Biden for the algae that had accumulated in its waters.

“This was in the Biden era … Look, it’s not an easy thing. The algae is brutal. It forms easily. All you saw was dirt and filth and paper and everything else for years,” Trump said on Monday.

Two days later, as the scale of his party’s staggering losses came into focus, Trump led a media tour of the White House Ballroom construction site, where he marveled at the renovations to come.

“The whole thing is a miracle,” he said.
output.standfirst: Donald Trump says repairs to the White House's deteriorated exterior are part of a wider renovation push, as he moves to shield his redesign of the Oval Office and Cabinet Room from change — a gesture that comes days after his party's landslide midterm defeat and renewed mockery from Barack Obama, who likened the gold-covered room to a Cheesecake Factory.
